sections.h2: How the university shapes Champaign sales
sections.html:
Champaign is a city in Champaign County in east-central Illinois. It shares the main University of Illinois campus with its twin city, Urbana. The 2020 census counted 88,302 residents, and the city covers 22.99 square miles of land.

The University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign enrolls more than 50,000 students a year, and Parkland College adds about 9,000. Whether a house sits near campus, near Parkland on the northwest side or out toward the newer southwest subdivisions changes who the likely buyer or tenant is. Check the Champaign Unit 4 attendance boundary before you advertise a school connection.

A single-family seller a few blocks from Campustown or downtown should expect buyers to ask about parking, noise and nearby rental density.

The university and health care dominate local jobs. The University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign has 13,934 employees and Carle Foundation Hospital has 6,921, and that mix with technology work tends to hold housing demand steady. Employees often want a short drive or a bus line, so say which applies to your house.

Interstates 57, 72 and 74 meet at or near Champaign, and Illinois Terminal is the hub for Amtrak, intercity buses and the local transit district. Houses near a bus line to campus are easy to describe to investors and to students' parents.

sections.h2: Showing a house during the school year
sections.html: Campus calendars drive local life. Semester start and finish dates bring waves of movers, and a house on the market near campus will see more traffic when students and staff are in town. Choose showing times that avoid move-in weeks, and keep rental tenants informed so they stay cooperative. If a tenant lives in the house, give the required notice before any visit and ask whether the lease allows photos.

Champaign sits on relatively high ground for the region, and downtown drains toward Boneyard Creek. If your street is near the creek, ask your insurer or the city about drainage, since a buyer's inspector will notice a wet basement.

The area has hot summers and cold winters, so inspectors tend to look at roofs, gutters, sump pumps, furnaces and air conditioners. A seller with an aging system can expect the issue to come up in negotiations. A cash buyer purchasing as-is usually prices it in directly.

sections.h2: When building work needs a permit
sections.html:
The city requires a permit whenever you build, enlarge, alter, repair, move or demolish a structure. The same goes for installing or replacing electrical, gas, mechanical, plumbing, sprinkler or fire alarm systems. Since January 1, 2025, applications go through an online portal. The city adopted the 2021 International Codes on January 9, 2024.

Champaign permit rules
Type of workPermit
New building, addition, alteration, repair, move or demolitionNeeded
Electrical, gas, mechanical, plumbing, sprinkler or fire alarm systemsNeeded
Sheds up to 120 square feetExempt
FencesExempt from a building permit, but zoning rules still apply
Playground equipment and minor repairsExempt

Check with the Building Safety Division before any project, and request the permit history on your address before listing. Buyers' inspectors and lenders may flag a permit nobody closed.

Property maintenance, nuisance and blight rules are enforced by the Neighborhood Code Compliance Division, and neighbors can file complaints with the city. An open complaint on your house should be cleared before you list.

The city has described a registry of residential rentals and vacant commercial buildings, meant to give it current owner and agent contact information. If you own a rental, ask the Neighborhood Services department whether registration has taken effect.

Downtown property owners should know about the snow rule. When public works declares the ordinance in effect after more than two inches of snow, owners in the designated areas have 24 hours to clear sidewalks, or the city clears them and bills the owner plus an administrative fee.

The state's transfer tax is 50 cents for every $500 of value, or fraction of $500, shown on the declaration (35 ILCS 200/31-10). Filing happens in MyDec, and its customer service line is 844-445-1114.

Your deed goes to the Champaign County recorder. Before a closing date is set, put one question to the recorder, the city and your title company: does any local transfer or utility step apply to this property?

sections.h2: Listing, selling yourself or taking a cash offer
sections.html:
A house in good repair, with an owner who can handle showings through the school year, does well on the open market. A property with deferred maintenance, or a rental aimed at students, can fit an investor who intends to renovate. Cash shortens the calendar and ends the repair haggling, though the price lands under what a finished house would earn.

Start every conversation with buyers armed with the permit history, utility details and any tenant lease.

sections.h2: Preparing a student rental for sale
sections.html:
A rental near campus carries extra paperwork. Gather the current lease, a rent roll if the building has several units, and repair records. Give buyers the lease end dates, since those decide when a new owner can move in or re-rent. Neighborhood Services can answer rental registration questions, and Neighborhood Code Compliance can report open complaints.

Investors who buy student housing think about turnover and condition. Give a cash buyer a plain list of what needs work and what you have replaced.

sections.h2: What to bring to your title company
sections.html:
• The deed and the most recent property tax information for the parcel.
  • Permit history, plus any repair receipts for the roof, furnace, plumbing or electrical work.
  • Current leases, if any tenant lives in the house.
  • Utility account details, so final readings can be arranged.
  • A note of any open complaint with Neighborhood Code Compliance.

Having this folder ready speeds up a title search and lets a cash buyer make a firm offer without a second visit. If something is missing, say so plainly, and tell the buyer who you called to find it. That honesty usually builds trust and keeps the deal moving.

sections.h2: Steps from signed contract to deed recording
sections.html:
Start by choosing a title company and giving it the contract. Complete the Illinois transfer declaration in MyDec. Check with the city for any local requirement tied to the property, such as a utility step. Then sign the deed and send it for recording with the Champaign County recorder.

Book each step in order and keep copies. If the house has open permit work or a code complaint, resolve it or agree in writing with the buyer who will take it on. A buyer who closes with cash does not wait on a lender, so the timeline depends mostly on how fast the title work and your paperwork move.

faqs.q: What is the largest employer in Champaign?
faqs.a: The University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign is the largest by a wide margin, and it shapes who buys and rents houses near campus.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for a shed or fence in Champaign?
faqs.a: Sheds up to 120 square feet and fences are exempt from building permits, but zoning rules still apply to fences. Ask the Building Safety Division before you build.

faqs.q: How do I report a property maintenance problem?
faqs.a: File a complaint with the Neighborhood Code Compliance Division of the City of Champaign. The division enforces property maintenance, nuisance and blight rules.

faqs.q: What is the Illinois transfer tax on a sale?
faqs.a: The state rate is 50 cents for each $500 of value or fraction of $500 stated in the transfer declaration. The declaration is completed in the state's MyDec system.

faqs.q: How many people live in Champaign?
faqs.a: The 2020 census counted 88,302 residents. That makes Champaign the tenth most populous municipality in Illinois.
